deep.reconstruction:
PURPOSE. The page prepares data for orbit computations for Ceres. It uses the observation that von Zach made on 1801 Dec 7 and recognised only later as Ceres, plus three observations from 1802. The four observations are: 1801 Dec 7, 1802 Jan 25, 1802 Mar 25 and 1802 May 23.

All positions are put into EQUATORIAL coordinates referred to the mean equinox of 1802.0. Only right ascensions are formed for the first and last observations; right ascension and declination are formed for the middle two. This is exactly the input of the problem 'orbit from four observations of which only two are complete', with the equator as fundamental plane. The next page continues with the node, the quantities a', b', c', d', e', a'', ... and P, 1+P', which supports this reading.

(1) TIME.
- 18h48'10.3" − 20'11.8" = 18h27'58.5" (Seeberg time; the nature of the 20'11.8" correction is not stated).
- Minus the Seeberg–Paris longitude difference 33'35" gives Paris 17h54'23.5" = 17h54.3917m.
- 54.3917/60 = 0.906528, so 17.906528 h; 17.906528/24 = 0.7461053, so Dec 7.7461053 Paris mean time.
- Times from the epoch 1801 Dec 31.0 (= 1802 Jan 0.0): t = −23.2538947, +25.6660347, +84.4951586, +143.2802916 days.
- Logs of the |t|: 1.3664957, 1.4093588, 1.9268318, 2.1561865 (the last corrected from a slip).
- With log(50.1"/365.25) ≈ 9.13725 these give precession in longitude: 3.19", 3.52", 11.59", 19.65".

(2) SUN.
- Mean longitude on Dec 7 is 255°44'44.76" (nutation +1.24" noted but not used).
- Adding precession +3.19" reduces it to 1802.0: 255°44'47.95".
- Likewise the Sun longitudes on the other dates: 305°33'35.38", 4°37'8.30", 61°49'40.17".
- Obliquity ε = 23°27'55.61", with log sin ε = 9.6000968, log cos ε = 9.9625116 and (implicitly) log tan ε = 9.6375852.
- Log Earth–Sun distance on Dec 7: first written 9.9646322 (wrong), corrected to 9.9932741.
- The other log R values are 9.9933838 (Jan 25), 9.9992672 (Mar 25), 0.0056917 (May 23).

(3) SUN'S EQUATORIAL COORDINATES (rows labelled I–IV = the four dates in order Dec, Jan, Mar, May).
- The listed numbers 0.1457731, 0.2711836, 0.5951153, 8.9073650 are log tan λ☉.
- Right ascension: tan A = cos ε tan λ☉. This gives A = 254°31'15.20", 307°55'47.88", 4°14'18.38", 59°43'16.60".
- Check via log cos D = log sin λ☉ + log cos ε − log sin A. Values: 9.9649780, 9.9759274, 9.9997766, 9.9714460.
- Declination: tan D = tan ε sin A, giving 9.6215396, 9.5345316, 8.5062724, 9.5738892.
- So D = −22°42'7.15", −18°54'4.01", +1°50'15.29", +20°32'59.58".
- Earth's heliocentric equatorial coordinates: l = A + 180°, so l = 74°31'15.20", l' = 127°55'47.88", l'' = 184°14'18.38", l''' = 239°43'16.60".
- Earth's heliocentric latitudes (relative to the equator) for the middle dates: B' = −D' = +18°54'4.01" and B'' = −D'' = −1°50'15.29".
- Projected distances log(R cos D): 9.9582521 (corrected from 9.9296102, which used the bad R), 9.9693112, 9.9990438, 9.9771377.
- Side computations log R cos B / cos B: 1.6894858, 1.7695924, 1.7692675 and 9.9250672, 0.0051738, 0.0048489 (purpose not fully clear).

(4) '2ter Ort': ecliptic to equatorial conversion with Gauss's auxiliary angle, for the Jan 25 geocentric place of Ceres.
- Input: λ = 182°49'51.82" and log tan β = 9.4051740 (β ≈ +14°15'51").
- tan N = tan β / sin λ: N = 79°0'15.69" (magnitudes used; signs handled implicitly).
- N − ε = 55°32'20.08".
- tan α = tan λ · cos(N−ε)/cos N: 8.6941802 + 9.7526986 − 9.2804289 = 9.1664499, so α' = 188°20'46.09".
- tan δ = tan(N−ε) sin α: 0.1634977 + 9.16182.. = 9.3253236, so δ' = b' = 11°56'32.71".
- Check cos δ cos α = cos β cos λ: log cos δ − log cos β = 9.9904970 − 9.9864032 = 0.0040938. This equals log cos λ − log cos α. (Gauss labels the 9.9904970 'cos δ'.)

(5) REDUCTION APPARENT TO MEAN (nutation, and probably aberration).
- The first row 11s25°49', 11s23°14', 11s20°8', 11s17°1' is the longitude of the Moon's node in signs. It regresses about 3.18'/day, matching the date intervals.
- A second argument is node + (1°3', 1°41', 2°26', 3°10').
- The four corrections +1.20", +1.94", +2.83", +3.71" equal Δψ cos ε with Δψ ≈ −18" sin Ω.
- Further terms involve log tan δ = 9.3200, 9.3253, 9.5048, 9.4218 (declinations ≈ 11.80°, 11.94°, 17.73°, 14.80°).
- Sums: RA corrections +0.26", +7.08", +16.40", +24.32"; declination corrections −3.87" (→ −3.60"), −15.37" (→ −6.06"), −8.97".
- The detailed meaning of the second and third terms is my inference.

(6) RESULTING DATA.
- t = −23.253895, +25.666035, +84.495159, +143.280292.
- Right ascensions: α = 178°33'30.34", α' = 188°20'46.12", α'' = 181°54'2.40", α''' = 176°49'50.68".
- Declinations: b' = 11°56'32.72", b'' = 17°43'58.82".
- Earth: l, l', l'', l''' as above; B' = +18°54'4.01", B'' = −1°50'15.29".
- Finally log tan b' = 9.3253237, log cos b' = 9.9904969, log tan b'' = 9.5048453, log cos b'' = 9.9788587.
- Differences: α' − l' = +60°24'58.24" and α'' − l'' = −2°20'15.98".
errors: Initial log Earth–Sun distance for Dec 7 (9.9646322) was wrong; Gauss struck it and replaced it by 9.9932741. The derived log R cos D (9.9296102) was replaced by 9.9582521. The next page uses 9.9582524.
log sin λ for λ = 188°20'46.09" is 9.1618270. The figure is overwritten in the manuscript; the sum 9.3253236 corresponds to log sin λ ≈ 9.16182(6). Any discrepancy is in the 7th decimal only.

In the declination corrections, two totals (−3.87, −15.37) are struck or replaced by −3.60 and −6.06. As transcribed, the components do not add up to the struck totals, so a term was apparently revised.
Quadrant/sign handling in the auxiliary-angle conversion is implicit: magnitudes of N and N−ε were used with sin λ < 0. The result (α in the 3rd quadrant, δ > 0) is correct.
The 20'11.8" time correction is unexplained on the page; I cannot verify it.

results.what: Conversion of observation time to Paris mean time and to days from epoch 1801 Dec 31.0; general precession at ~50.1"/yr applied to reduce longitudes to equinox 1802.0

Sun's right ascension and declination from its longitude: tan A = cos ε tan λ, tan D = tan ε sin A, with check cos D sin A = cos ε sin λ; Earth's heliocentric equatorial coordinates l = A+180°, B = −D
results.modern_name: ecliptic–equatorial transformation for a point on the ecliptic

results.what: Ecliptic to equatorial transformation of Ceres's place via the auxiliary angle N (tan N = tan β/sin λ; tan α = tan λ cos(N−ε)/cos N; tan δ = tan(N−ε) sin α), with control equation cos δ cos α = cos β cos λ
results.modern_name: coordinate transformation with auxiliary angle (Gauss's logarithmic form)
results.usually_credited_to: classical; this auxiliary-angle form is standard (also in Gauss's Theoria Motus)

results.what: Nutation (and probably aberration) corrections in RA/Dec using the longitude of the lunar node
results.modern_name: reduction from apparent to mean place

results.what: Assembly of data (four RAs, two declinations, Earth's heliocentric equatorial coordinates) for orbit determination from four observations of which only the middle two are complete, using the equator as reference plane, for Ceres including Zach's 1801 Dec 7 observation
results.modern_name: Gauss's four-observation method (Theoria Motus, Book II, Sect. II)

deep.surprise_reason: Routine numerical working: reductions and coordinate transformations preparing a known Gaussian method (four observations, two complete). The only mild interest is the documented use of Zach's retroactively identified 1801 Dec 7 Ceres observation and the equator as reference plane. Whether this exact computation corresponds to a published example is uncertain.

The Roman-numeral entries 18.54.4.01, 20.32.59.58, 22.42.7.15, 1.50.15.29 are Sun declinations (deg/min/sec), not times.
